body:
Why spent fuel remains hazardous

Nuclear fuel does not become harmless when it is removed from a reactor. Spent nuclear fuel contains radioactive fission products, other radionuclides and remaining nuclear material. It continues to emit radiation and produce decay heat.

Spent fuel therefore requires shielding, cooling, confinement, monitoring and secure handling. Its eventual management depends partly on whether the country chooses to recover usable nuclear material or to manage the spent fuel directly as waste.

Wet storage in spent-fuel pools

Spent fuel is commonly transferred first to a specially designed water-filled storage pool. The water performs 2 major functions: it removes decay heat and provides shielding against radiation.

Pool storage also involves arrangements for water quality, monitoring and maintaining safe conditions. The pool is an engineered nuclear storage facility, not an ordinary water reservoir.

The amount of heat generated by spent fuel generally decreases with time as radionuclides decay. This reduction is important when considering later storage options.

Dry storage in protected containers

After sufficient cooling, suitable spent fuel may be placed in specially designed dry storage casks or other approved dry-storage systems. These typically use sealed containers and substantial shielding to control radiation exposure and the release of radioactive material.

Dry-storage systems commonly dissipate residual heat through passive mechanisms such as conduction, radiation and natural air circulation. Their safety still depends on correct design, loading, inspection, monitoring and protection from external hazards.

Wet storage uses water for cooling and shielding. Dry storage uses engineered containers and shielding, with heat removal commonly relying on passive processes. Both are storage arrangements, not automatic final disposal methods.

The difference between storage and disposal

Storage keeps radioactive material in a facility with the intention that it can be retrieved for further management, treatment, reprocessing or eventual disposal. It therefore requires continuing safety arrangements and oversight.

Disposal means placing waste in an appropriate facility without the intention of retrieving it. Its long-term safety must be demonstrated using suitable barriers and site characteristics.

Storage can last for years or longer, but the passage of time does not by itself turn storage into disposal. A dry storage cask is not necessarily a deep geological repository.

What is nuclear-fuel reprocessing?

Reprocessing separates potentially reusable nuclear materials from the products remaining in spent fuel. In a closed fuel-cycle approach, recovered materials can be used for further nuclear-fuel production, subject to the applicable processes and controls.

India follows a fuel-cycle strategy that includes reprocessing and recovery of useful nuclear materials. Reprocessing can recover material for reuse, but it does not eliminate the radioactive-waste problem. The remaining streams include highly radioactive residues requiring further treatment, conditioning, storage and eventual disposal.

Direct disposal and reprocessing are different pathways

In an open or once-through fuel cycle, spent fuel is treated as material for eventual disposal after appropriate storage and preparation. In a closed fuel cycle, spent fuel is reprocessed to recover useful nuclear material, while radioactive residues continue through the waste-management system.

Neither pathway makes nuclear safety unnecessary. Both require continuing control of radiation exposure and the movement of radioactive substances.

Prelims focus

  • Spent nuclear fuel remains radioactive and generates decay heat after removal from a reactor.
  • Water in a spent-fuel pool provides both cooling and radiation shielding.
  • Dry casks provide engineered confinement and shielding for suitable cooled fuel.
  • Storage is intended to permit retrieval; disposal does not rely on planned retrieval.
  • Reprocessing recovers potentially reusable nuclear material but leaves radioactive residues.
  • Trap: Reprocessing does not make all radioactive waste disappear.

[Sources: IAEA, Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel, sections on wet storage, dry storage and Annex I, paragraphs I.62–I.64 (consulted 16 November 2026); Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Radioactive Waste Management: Indian Scenario, high-level-waste management section (consulted 16 November 2026); Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Research and Development Activities: Reprocessing and Nuclear Waste Management, sections on fuel reprocessing and high-level liquid waste (consulted 16 November 2026).]

title: Spent Nuclear Fuel: Wet Storage, Dry Storage and Reprocessing

body:
The stages of radioactive-waste management

Radioactive-waste management begins before waste is placed in a storage or disposal facility. Waste must first be identified and characterized so that an appropriate method can be selected. Important information includes its radioactivity, radionuclides, physical state, heat generation and expected behaviour over time.

The main stages are:

  1. Minimization and segregation: Reduce the amount of waste generated and separate waste streams according to their characteristics.
  2. Characterization: Determine the relevant physical, chemical and radiological properties.
  3. Treatment: Change the waste or reduce its volume to make further management safer or more efficient.
  4. Conditioning: Convert the waste into a form suitable for handling, transport, storage or disposal, often by immobilizing it and placing it in a suitable container.
  5. Storage: Hold the waste safely while monitoring it or awaiting further management.
  6. Disposal: Place suitable waste in an approved disposal facility designed to provide long-term protection.

Examples of treatment methods include filtration, evaporation and ion exchange for suitable liquid waste streams, and compaction for certain solid wastes. Conditioning can include immobilizing waste in cement or glass and sealing it inside appropriate packages.

Three broad waste-management principles

Indian radioactive-waste management guidance describes 3 important approaches:

  • Delay and decay: Retain short-lived radioactive waste under control until its activity has fallen sufficiently for an approved subsequent management route.
  • Concentrate and contain: Collect and immobilize radioactivity in a controlled waste form and prevent its uncontrolled movement into the environment.
  • Dilute and disperse within authorized limits: Permit appropriate low-activity discharges only when regulatory requirements, monitoring and discharge authorizations are satisfied.

These principles apply to different waste situations. They are not interchangeable instructions to mix or release radioactive material indiscriminately.

Vitrification of high-level liquid waste

Reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel produces high-level liquid waste containing highly radioactive residues. This liquid cannot simply be treated like ordinary industrial wastewater.

Vitrification immobilizes suitable high-level liquid waste in a glass matrix, commonly based on borosilicate glass. The resulting solid glass form is placed in an appropriate container and managed under controlled conditions.

The purpose is to make radioactive constituents less mobile and produce a stable waste form that can be handled, stored and eventually placed in a suitable disposal facility.

Vitrification is immobilization, not elimination of radioactivity. The vitrified material remains radioactive, may continue to produce decay heat and still requires shielding, controlled storage and an appropriate long-term disposal pathway.

How disposal methods differ by waste type

Waste containing predominantly short-lived radionuclides and limited long-lived activity can often be managed through suitable engineered near-surface disposal facilities, provided the applicable waste-acceptance criteria are met.

Near-surface facilities may use engineered trenches, concrete vaults, approved waste packages, backfill and covers. Their design aims to restrict water movement, protect the waste and reduce the possibility of radionuclides reaching people or the environment.

Waste with larger quantities of long-lived radionuclides may require disposal at greater depth. High-level waste, because of its radioactivity, longevity and possible decay-heat generation, generally requires a deep geological disposal approach for long-term isolation.

Deep geological repositories

A deep geological repository is a facility intended to isolate radioactive waste within a suitable stable geological formation. It combines engineered barriers with the protective properties of the surrounding rock.

Depending on the disposal concept, engineered barriers may include the solid waste form, metal containers, seals, backfill and specially selected materials that restrict water movement. The surrounding geological formation supplies additional isolation by limiting the movement of water and radionuclides.

A suitable repository must be selected and assessed with reference to geological conditions, groundwater behaviour, long-term stability and possible disturbance by human activity. Geological disposal commonly involves depths of hundreds of metres, but 500 metres is not a universal compulsory depth for all repositories.

The key requirement is demonstrated long-term safety, not merely placing containers underground. A disposal facility must remain acceptably safe without depending indefinitely on future generations operating pumps, repairing barriers or maintaining constant supervision.

Conditioning, storage and disposal must not be confused

A vitrified waste container is a conditioned waste package. A monitored vault holding that package is an interim storage facility. An approved geological repository receiving suitable waste for permanent isolation is a disposal facility.

These terms describe different purposes and stages. Their distinction is central to understanding radioactive-waste management.

Prelims focus

  • Treatment changes waste characteristics; conditioning prepares a suitable waste form or package.
  • Vitrification immobilizes high-level liquid waste in glass, commonly borosilicate glass.
  • Near-surface disposal generally suits appropriately characterized VLLW and LLW.
  • High-level waste generally requires long-term isolation through deep geological disposal.
  • Disposal safety depends on suitable engineered barriers and natural geological conditions.
  • Trap: A vitrified waste container in interim storage has not thereby undergone final geological disposal.

[Sources: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Radioactive Waste Management: Indian Scenario, sections on waste treatment, low-level waste and high-level waste (consulted 16 November 2026); Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Research and Development Activities: Reprocessing and Nuclear Waste Management, vitrification section (consulted 16 November 2026); Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Radioactive Waste Management, management philosophy and authorization sections (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, Near Surface Disposal Facilities for Radioactive Waste, sections 2, 4 and 7, including paragraphs 4.7 and 4.21 (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, IAEA-TECDOC-1740 (2014), Annex VIII, waste-classification and disposal-options discussion.]

pictures.caption: Different waste classes require different levels of containment and isolation.

pictures.alt: Nested engineered barriers within stable host rock restrict groundwater contact with radioactive waste and help isolate radionuclides from people and the environment.

title: Treatment, Vitrification and Final Disposal of Radioactive Waste

body:
Why radioactive-waste governance must continue over time

Some radioactive waste remains hazardous beyond the operating life of the installation where it was produced. Safe management therefore requires decisions that extend across storage, transport, disposal, monitoring, institutional responsibilities and the protection of future generations.

The organization generating or managing the waste must maintain appropriate records of its origin, radioactivity, composition, conditioning and location. These records support safe handling, regulatory inspection, eventual transfer to a disposal facility and long-term knowledge of what has been placed at a site.

A safety case is the collection of scientific evidence and technical arguments used to demonstrate that a facility can meet safety requirements. For a disposal facility, this includes consideration of waste characteristics, engineered barriers, geological conditions, possible exposure pathways and safety over relevant future periods.

The role of institutional control

Institutional control refers to administrative measures such as restricting access, preserving records, maintaining site information and monitoring a disposal location. Such measures are particularly important while a facility is operating and during applicable periods following closure.

However, deep geological disposal is intended to provide passive long-term safety. Its safety should not depend on an assumption that every future generation will continuously maintain equipment, repair containers or guard the site.

Monitoring provides information about safety; engineered and natural barriers provide the main long-term isolation. Monitoring cannot replace an unsuitable site or an inadequate disposal design.

Radioactive-waste management in India

India's nuclear-waste management system includes waste minimization, segregation, treatment, conditioning, safe storage and authorized disposal arrangements. AERB establishes and enforces relevant safety requirements, while the responsible facility organizations implement them.

For suitable low-level and intermediate-level waste streams, Indian facilities employ approved treatment and disposal methods that include engineered near-surface disposal facilities. Depending on the waste and authorization, such facilities may use stone-lined trenches, reinforced-concrete trenches or other engineered disposal structures.

Highly radioactive liquid residues arising from spent-fuel reprocessing are managed differently. They are immobilized through vitrification and stored under controlled conditions, with cooling and surveillance as necessary, pending a suitable final disposal route.

Important Indian locations for vitrification

BARC identifies operational high-level-waste vitrification facilities developed in India at the following locations:

  • Trombay: Maharashtra.
  • Tarapur: Maharashtra.
  • Kalpakkam: Tamil Nadu.

These locations are associated with the immobilization of high-level radioactive waste. They should not be confused with a claim that India already has an operating final deep geological repository for such waste. The BARC-described management pathway includes vitrification, monitored interim storage and eventual geological disposal.

Gujarat connection: Kakrapar Atomic Power Station

Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS) is situated in Gujarat near Surat. It is an important example of nuclear electricity generation within the state and helps connect national safety principles with an actual operating nuclear installation.

According to NPCIL's operating-performance information available in 2026, Kakrapar has 4 commercially operating pressurized heavy-water reactor (PHWR) units, with a total installed electrical capacity of 1840 MWe.

Kakrapar unitCapacity (MWe)Commercial operation began
KAPS Unit 12206 May 1993
KAPS Unit 22201 September 1995
KAPS Unit 370030 June 2023
KAPS Unit 470031 March 2024

These dates describe the beginning of commercial operation, not necessarily the date of first criticality, first power generation or construction approval. Those milestones are different.

Like other licensed nuclear installations, Kakrapar must implement applicable safety systems, radiation monitoring, emergency arrangements and radioactive-waste controls. The presence of a nuclear power station in Gujarat does not mean every national waste-treatment technology is located at that station.

Verified time reference: NPCIL's operating-performance listing for the financial year 2026–27 included plant-generation information through August 2026. The 4 Kakrapar unit capacities and commercial-operation dates stated above are drawn from that listing, consulted on 16 November 2026.

How safety and waste management fit together

Nuclear safety and radioactive-waste management are connected across the lifetime of a nuclear facility. Safe operation limits accidents and unnecessary radioactive releases. Waste minimization reduces the quantity requiring control. Characterization determines the correct management route. Appropriate storage keeps radioactive material controlled until the next stage. Suitable disposal provides long-term protection after active use has ended.

The underlying principle is the same throughout: radioactive substances must be controlled according to the risks they present, with several reliable protective measures and clear institutional responsibility.

Prelims focus

  • India's identified high-level-waste vitrification locations include Trombay, Tarapur and Kalpakkam.
  • Vitrified high-level waste undergoes controlled interim storage before eventual geological disposal.
  • Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is in Gujarat near Surat.
  • KAPS has 4 operating PHWR units with capacities of 220, 220, 700 and 700 MWe, totalling 1840 MWe in NPCIL's 2026 listing.
  • Long-term repository safety relies on engineered and natural barriers, not permanent active supervision alone.
  • Trap: Commercial operation, first criticality and first electricity generation are different milestones.

[Sources: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Radioactive Waste Management: Indian Scenario, near-surface disposal, vitrification and interim-storage sections (consulted 16 November 2026); Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Research and Development Activities: Reprocessing and Nuclear Waste Management, operational vitrification facilities (consulted 16 November 2026); Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, Operating Performance, FY 2026–27, information through August 2026, and All Nuclear Power Plants Details and Installed Capacity (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, Near Surface Disposal Facilities for Radioactive Waste, sections 4 and 7 on long-term safety and institutional control (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA, Fundamental Safety Principles, SF-1, Principle 7, Protection of Present and Future Generations.]

title: Radioactive-Waste Governance in India and the Gujarat Connection
